readerTitle: The bakery sign that told the truth and still sold nothing
caseNote: 가상 사례 (동네 빵집, 병원 예약 앱) + 마케팅계에 전해지는 드릴 비유 일화
insight: 기능은 믿을 근거이고, 이익은 살 이유다. 좋은 문장은 "so you can"으로 둘을 이어 손님의 하루에 일어나는 변화를 말한다.
misconception: 기능을 많이 나열하면 잘 팔린다. 반대로 기능을 빼고 감성적인 이익만 말하면 된다.

sources.text: Levitt, T. (1983). The Marketing Imagination. Levitt attributes the drill and hole line to Leo McGinneva.
빵집과 예약 앱 사례는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 드릴 비유의 출처를 확인하세요. 흔히 Theodore Levitt의 말로 알려져 있지만, Levitt는 『The Marketing Imagination』(1983)에서 Leo McGinneva의 말로 인용했습니다. 카드에서는 일화로 표시하고 "often credited to"라고 적었습니다.
"장시간 발효한 사워도우가 상온에서 더 오래 신선하다"는 일반적으로 알려진 내용이지만 레시피마다 다릅니다. 가상 사례이므로 구체적인 일수를 넣지 않고 "for days"로만 적었습니다. 소화가 잘된다는 식의 건강 주장은 일부러 넣지 않았습니다.
예약 앱 사례에는 노쇼 감소율 같은 수치를 넣지 않았습니다. 실제 수치를 넣으려면 출처가 필요합니다.

cards.title: The bakery sign that told the truth and still sold nothing
body: A baker spends two days on each loaf. Her chalkboard says so: *48-hour natural fermentation. Stone-milled flour. No additives.*
Every word is true. People read it, nod and buy the cheaper bread next door.

image.label: Chalkboard sign outside a bakery, passersby walking on
image.brief: 따뜻한 일러스트. 작은 빵집 앞 칠판 간판에 "48-hour natural fermentation / Stone-milled flour / No additives". 행인 두세 명이 힐끗 보고 지나감. 실제 브랜드나 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Rewrite the sign.
body: The baker has room for one line. Which one would you write?

options.text: Keep the facts and add more: hydration level, flour origin, oven type
options.feedback: Bread lovers might enjoy it. Most passersby would have to work out for themselves why any of it matters, and few will.
It talks about the customer, which helps. But every bakery could say it, so there's nothing to believe.

options.text: "Slow-fermented for 48 hours, so it stays fresh on your counter for days."
options.feedback: It names a real change in the customer's week and gives the reason to believe it. You lose some poetry and gain a reason to buy.

cards.title: The obvious fix failed too.
body: After the fact list flopped, the baker swung the other way. The new sign was warm and vague: *Bread that makes your mornings better.* People still walked past. It sounded like every other bakery.
The third sign did both jobs. It kept the 48 hours and added what they mean at home: bread that's still good on Thursday. Now people stopped and asked about it.

image.label: Three versions of the sign side by side
image.brief: 칠판 간판 세 개를 나란히. 1번은 기능 목록, 2번은 "Bread that makes your mornings better", 3번은 "Slow-fermented for 48 hours, so it stays fresh on your counter for days". 3번 앞에만 손님이 멈춰 있음.

cards.title: Features vs benefits
body: A **feature** is what your product is or has: 48-hour fermentation, a stainless steel blade, an hourly backup.
A **benefit** is what changes for the customer because of it: fresh bread on Thursday, a knife that stays sharp, no lost work.
Customers buy benefits. But they believe benefits because of features. A feature alone is proof with no point. A benefit alone is a point with no proof.

cards.title: Ask "so what?" until you reach the customer.
body: Marketers often cite a line credited to Theodore Levitt. By his own account he borrowed it from someone else: people don't want a quarter-inch drill, they want a quarter-inch hole. To get from drill to hole, keep asking *so what?*
list: *So what?* **You don't have to shop for bread every day**
cards.callout: Then join the ends: feature, plus "so you can," plus benefit.

cards.title: For some buyers, the feature is the benefit.
body: A chef buying an oven wants the exact temperature range. An engineer comparing parts wants the spec sheet. Experts already know what the numbers mean, so translating them can sound like you think they don't.
Know who's reading. Lead with benefits for people who are new to the category. Lead with features for people who compare products line by line, and keep the benefit close by.

cards.title: A benefit is a promise.
body: The jump from feature to benefit is where exaggeration creeps in. "Slow-fermented" can quietly become "healthier" or "easier to digest," claims the baker may not be able to back up.

Only promise the change your feature reliably delivers. If you can't say *because of what*, you're making a slogan, not stating a benefit. Customers notice when you overpromise, and the trust you lose is hard to win back.

cards.title: Now it's a booking app for clinics.
body: Your software sends patients a text the day before their appointment. You're writing the headline for your homepage, aimed at small clinic owners.

options.text: "Automated SMS reminders with custom templates and two-way replies."
options.feedback: Accurate and complete, but the clinic owner has to work out what it does for their day. Many won't bother.
It hits a real pain, but it doesn't say how. It reads like any competitor's ad.

options.text: "Texts each patient the day before, so fewer appointments are missed."
options.feedback: The feature makes the promise believable, and the benefit shows why it matters. You trade a punchier line for one people trust.

cards.title: Say what it is, then what it changes.
body: Features give customers a reason to believe. Benefits give them a reason to buy. Join the two with "so you can."
**Try it today:** take one line from your menu, sign or website. Ask "so what?" twice, then rewrite it as feature + so you can + benefit.
